blogs.title: Intrinsic Acts vs. Propensity: The Eighth Circuit's Expansive View of 'Continuous Possession' in Felon-in-Possession Cases
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's treatment of Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b) regarding the admission of prior sightings of the firearm. It examines the Eighth Circuit's reliance on *United States v. Battle* to classify evidence of previous possession as 'intrinsic' rather than character evidence, effectively creating a 'continuous possession' doctrine that allows prosecutors to introduce highly prejudicial prior acts without the strict safeguards usually required for propensity evidence. The analysis will explore the tension between proving an element of the crime (possession) and the risk of jurors convicting based on the defendant's history with weapons.

blogs.title: The Hollow Shield: Why 'Harmless Error' Analysis Renders Evidentiary Objections Futile in High-Stakes ACCA Prosecutions
blogs.description: Focusing on Section II(E) of the opinion, this article critiques the appellate court's application of the harmless error standard. Despite identifying potential issues—such as the admission of emotional testimony regarding a witness's sister killed by a gun and disputes over authenticating police reports for impeachment—the court affirmed the conviction because the remaining evidence was 'substantial.' The post argues that in cases involving egregious facts like those against Cutbank (domestic terrorism, sawed-off rifles), the harmless error doctrine effectively insulates district courts from reversal even when they stretch evidentiary rules, raising concerns about the practical viability of preserving trial errors for appeal.

blogs.title: Double Counting Danger? Navigating the Intersection of AC CA Mandates and USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancements
blogs.description: This post dissects the sentencing argument where Cutbank challenged the four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm 'in connection with another felony' alongside the mandatory Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) minimum. While the Eighth Circuit dismissed the argument as a challenge to substantive reasonableness rather than procedural error, this analysis explores the doctrinal friction between statutory mandatory minimums and guideline enhancements that may overlap factually. It discusses whether applying both mechanisms risks impermissible double-counting of the underlying violent conduct and how appellate courts are increasingly deferring to district judges' discretion under *Gall* and § 3553(a) to resolve these tensions without altering calculation methodologies.
